# Part A Project Overview and Business Rules (Jaden)

**JACPot** is a proposed local marketplace for students at John Abbott College. It will bring listings, item requests, and student communication into one campus-focused application. Students will be able to sell items they no longer need, find second-hand alternatives, and arrange exchanges with other students.

General marketplaces serve broad audiences, which can make it difficult to find relevant items nearby. The team also finds existing textbook exchanges too limited for students who want to trade school supplies, clothing, electronics, and hobby items. **JACPot** addresses this gap by organizing buying and selling around the John Abbott community.

Students will browse or search listings, contact sellers, and agree on a price and campus meetup location. If an item is unavailable, they can post a request that other students can answer. Registration through a John Abbott College email address and accounts linked to student identities are intended to support accountability, although these measures cannot eliminate fraud or guarantee safe exchanges.

As John Abbott students, we have experienced the difficulty of finding suitable marketplace listings and have kept expensive textbooks after their courses ended. We want to build an application that we would use ourselves: a clear, practical way to connect students who have items with students who need them.

## 1     Expected Benefits and Shared Data Rules (Chris)

**JACPot** is intended to help students reduce spending by finding second-hand textbooks, supplies, clothing, and other items. Sellers can recover some of their original costs, while buyers can compare available alternatives to retail purchases. Reusing items can also reduce waste, and on-campus exchanges can reduce the need for shipping and packaging. These are expected benefits rather than measured outcomes.

Every user must register with a valid @johnabbottcollege.net email address and complete student account verification. Listings and item requests remain associated with their creators, and only their owners may modify or remove them. Conversations link exactly two participating students to the listing or request that initiated the discussion. The backend will enforce account ownership and access permissions consistently across the platform.

## 2 Feature Business Rules

### 2.1 Listings (Jaden)

Each listing must belong to a verified student account and include a title, description, condition, category, and positive asking price in Canadian dollars. Students may upload up to five photos, with the first used as the cover image. Category-specific fields will provide relevant details; for books, these may include author, release date, course code, and whether an online access code has been used. Buyers contact sellers through chat to discuss the exchange. Owners can edit their listings, mark them as sold, or delete them. Sold and deleted listings will no longer appear in active browsing or search results.

### 2.2 Chat and Messaging (Chris)

Each conversation connects two verified students through an active listing or item request. Only those participants may view the conversation or send messages. The conversation identifies the buyer, seller, and associated item, and retains its message history. Students can discuss condition, price, and meetup arrangements, using designated campus zones for exchanges. A Buy Request records a proposed price in CAD and a campus meetup location. Its price must be zero or greater, allowing a negotiated exchange to be free. The seller must explicitly accept the offer before it is recorded as agreed.

### 2.3 Item Requests (Luca)

Each item request must belong to a verified student account and include a title and description. Students must provide at least one of a course code or maximum budget. A supplied budget must be a positive amount in CAD. Requests remain active for 30 days, or until an optional needed-by date passes, unless the owner closes them or marks them as fulfilled earlier. Only the owner may edit, close, delete, or mark a request as fulfilled.

The AI chat bar asks clarifying questions to identify the item and checks active listings for a relevant match. If a match exists, it directs the student to that listing. Otherwise, it prepares a request draft for the student to review before posting. AI-generated requests follow the same validation rules as manually created requests. Price suggestions are an optional enhancement.

# Part B Interface Design and Application Features

## 1 Design and Technical Architecture (Luca)

### 1.1 Visual Design

**JACPot** will use a clean, approachable interface based on Material 3. Familiar buttons, cards, text fields, and navigation patterns will help students browse items, create posts, and communicate with minimal effort. Consistent layouts and clear headings will make each screen’s purpose and available actions easy to understand.

The design will use white and light gray backgrounds with dark, readable text. John Abbott’s blue (#0055A3) will identify primary actions, links, and selected navigation items, while yellow (#FFF001) will appear sparingly in highlights such as AI-assistance labels. Dark text will be used on yellow backgrounds, and labels and icons will support colour cues.

Typography and spacing will establish a clear hierarchy. Large headings will identify screens, item titles will stand out within cards, and supporting text will present prices, conditions, course codes, and posting times. Rounded cards and lightly outlined fields will organize information without making the interface feel crowded. Listing cards will emphasize images and prices, while request cards will emphasize the item needed, budget, and course information.

Responsive layouts will use a persistent bottom navigation bar on mobile and a navigation rail on larger screens. Content widths and spacing will adapt to the available space while preserving entered information. Accessibility will be supported through comfortable touch targets, labelled controls, and layouts that accommodate larger text. Clear loading, empty, and error states will explain what is happening and offer practical next steps, such as creating a request when no matching listings appear.

### 1.2 Technical Architecture

**JACPot** will use Kotlin Multiplatform to share application logic and data models across supported platforms. Compose Multiplatform will provide the interface through reusable components such as listing cards, request forms, and navigation controls. This will reduce duplicated code and maintain consistency across the app.

State hoisting will separate reusable interface components from the information they display. Shared state and business logic will be managed through ViewModels, while components receive values and callbacks. rememberSaveable will preserve lightweight interface state, such as search text and selected filters, across supported recreation events. Permanent records will be stored in the database rather than relying on interface state.

Ktor Client will handle communication between the app and its backend. Ktor Server will process registration, login, account permissions, listings, and requests, with WebSocket connections supporting real-time messaging. Network operations will use Kotlin coroutines to keep the interface responsive while information is being sent or retrieved.

Supabase will provide persistent storage for student accounts, listings, requests, conversations, and messages. Each record will use identifiers to connect it to the appropriate student and related content. The app will access Supabase through the Ktor backend, which will validate information and enforce permissions. Database credentials will remain on the server, and passwords will be stored as secure hashes.

Kamel will load and cache listing photos and student profile pictures within the Compose interface. Loading indicators and fallback images will provide feedback when an image is unavailable. Together, these tools will separate interface design, state management, networking, and storage into manageable parts of the application.

## 2 Pillar One Browsing and Listings (Jaden)

Listing and Home Screen Mockups

### 2.1 Home and Navigation

The Home screen introduces the main workflows through a search field, an entry point to advanced search, shortcuts to create a listing or request, and a feed of recently posted items. These elements give students a direct route to buying, selling, or requesting an item.

The account control in the upper-right corner will display the student’s first name or, if implemented, a profile picture. It opens an account panel showing the student’s name and email, with options to log out and change their password. Profile picture management is optional. Navigation provides access to Home, Listings, Requests, and Chat, adapting to the available screen size.

### 2.2 Core Features

Pillar One covers the full listing lifecycle, from creating a post to browsing available items and managing a completed sale.

Listing creation. Students enter a title, description, category, condition, and positive asking price in CAD. A course code is optional, and book listings expose additional category-specific fields. The form accepts up to five photos and uses the first as its cover. Inline validation explains errors before publication, and the backend applies the same validation rules.

Responsive listing feed. Material 3 cards emphasize item photos and prices. Kamel will load images asynchronously with loading indicators and fallback images. Layouts use one column below 600 dp and an adaptive grid at 600 dp and above, with width and aspect-ratio constraints to keep cards readable.

Listing details and management. Selecting a card opens a Material 3 detail dialog showing the item description, seller information, course details, and photos. A Message Seller action starts a conversation. Owners can edit the listing, mark it as sold, or delete it. Deletion requires confirmation.

### 2.3 AI Level Up Advanced Search

The advanced search feature will interpret everyday language as a combination of keywords and filters. The team plans to use AI development tools to help implement and test the parser, while retaining responsibility for its behaviour and validation.

The parser will combine keyword extraction, fuzzy matching, price-limit detection, and recognition of course codes or class references. This is a planned development enhancement; its accuracy will be tested against representative student queries, with standard keyword matching available when interpretation is uncertain.

For example, “Calculators under $25” should identify calculators as the item and $25 CAD as the maximum price. A query such as “Book for English class” should use available course and listing information to identify relevant results. The search must not assume a specific course code when the wording is ambiguous.

A Smart Search banner above the results will show the interpreted criteria, such as “Calculators — Up to $25 CAD.” Students can review and clear incorrectly interpreted filters. This feedback makes the search interpretation visible and helps students refine their results.

## 3 Pillar Two Authentication and Messaging (Chris)

Chat and Login Screen Mockups

### 3.1 Core Features

The Login and Create Account screens provide students with secure access to **JACPot**. During registration, users must provide a valid @johnabbottcollege.net email address to verify their affiliation with John Abbott College and create an account linked to their identity. Returning users can log in using their registered credentials to access their listings, chats, and item requests. All marketplace activity is associated with the relevant student account, so that conversations, listings, and requests remain traceable to their creators. These screens establish the authentication and account ownership requirements necessary to protect user access and maintain accountability throughout the platform.

The chat feature allows students to communicate directly with one another about active listings and item requests. Each conversation is associated with two verified **JACPot** student accounts and is initiated through a listing or request. This provides context for the discussion and helps both participants understand which item the conversation concerns. The chat identifies the buyer and seller and maintains a link to the original listing or request, allowing users to refer back to the item's details throughout the negotiation.

The Chat screen provides a simple messaging interface where buyers and sellers can exchange text messages and review their complete conversation history. Students can discuss item condition, availability, pricing, and meetup arrangements without needing to switch to an external messaging platform. For example, a buyer interested in a used textbook can ask about its condition, negotiate a lower price, and coordinate a convenient time to collect it. Keeping these discussions within **JACPot** helps users track the details they have discussed and reduces the need to share personal contact information.

To encourage safe and convenient exchanges, users arrange meetups at designated campus zones. These locations provide familiar places for students to exchange items while reducing the need to share private addresses. Buyers and sellers can discuss their preferred location and meeting time through the conversation and refer to their messages when coordinating the exchange.

Access to each conversation is restricted to its two participating students. Only the buyer and seller involved in the original listing or request can view and send messages, helping protect private negotiations and transaction details. Together, these features provide a centralized space for communication and coordination, supporting **JACPot**'s goal of creating a convenient and safer student marketplace.

### 3.2 AI Level Up Structured Buy Requests

The proposed messaging enhancement is a Buy Request widget that records transaction terms within an existing conversation. Buyers enter a proposed price in CAD and select a designated campus meetup zone, giving both students a clear offer to review.

When a buyer is ready to make an offer, they can create a Buy Request by entering their proposed price and selecting a meetup location. The price must be zero or greater, allowing students to offer items for free while preventing invalid negative amounts. Once submitted, the widget appears within the conversation and displays the proposed price and meetup location. For example, a buyer interested in a textbook could send a Buy Request displaying **$30 CAD** and **John Abbott Library Entrance** as the proposed meetup location.

The seller can review the widget and accept the offer by clicking the **Accept Offer** button. If the seller does not agree with the proposed terms, they can decline the request and continue negotiating through regular chat messages. The buyer can then submit another Buy Request with an updated price or meetup location. Sending a request does not automatically confirm a transaction; the offer becomes accepted only when the seller explicitly accepts it.

Once accepted, the Buy Request retains the agreed-upon price and meetup location within the conversation history, allowing both students to refer back to the transaction details. The widget should clearly distinguish between pending, accepted, and declined requests so that users can understand the current status of an offer. If the buyer and seller agree to different terms, a new request should be created rather than silently changing an already accepted agreement.

The Buy Request widget builds on **JACPot**'s existing messaging functionality by turning important transaction details into a structured, actionable element within the conversation. This makes offers easier to review than scattered text messages and reduces ambiguity about the proposed price and meeting arrangements. The feature does not process payments or automatically verify that an exchange has taken place; it records the participants' agreement to the proposed terms. Overall, the widget provides a straightforward way for students to negotiate, accept offers, and keep track of their transaction details without leaving the chat.

## 4 Pillar Three Item Requests (Luca)

### 4.1 Core Features

The request feature gives students a way to find items that are not currently available in JACPot’s listings. Instead of repeatedly searching the marketplace, a student can publish a request describing what they need. Other students can then discover that request and respond if they have a suitable item. This creates a reverse marketplace where demand is visible alongside items offered for sale.

The **Create Request** screen provides a structured form for entering an item title, description, and at least one of a course code or maximum budget. The title identifies the item, while the description communicates requirements such as a textbook edition, calculator model, size, or acceptable condition. A course code helps connect requests to specific classes, while a maximum budget helps potential sellers understand the requester’s spending limit. Students can also provide a needed-by date to communicate when they require the item. Clearly labelled fields and inline validation messages help students submit useful requests without losing their progress when correcting an error.

The **Browse Requests** screen displays active requests in a searchable feed. Each card presents the item title, relevant course information, budget when provided, and posting time. Students can quickly scan these details before opening a request to read its complete description. Searching by item name or course code helps students identify requests they may be able to fulfil. For example, a student who has finished an English course could search for its code and find someone looking for the same textbook.

From an active request’s detailed view, another verified student can contact the requester through JACPot’s messaging feature. The conversation remains linked to the original request so both participants can refer to the item and its requirements while discussing price, condition, and pickup arrangements. Responding to a request does not automatically confirm a sale; both students must agree on the exchange.

Request owners can edit their information, close a request, delete it, or mark it as fulfilled once they obtain the item. Requests expire after 30 days, or earlier if their needed-by date passes, keeping outdated entries out of the active feed. Together, these features help students communicate their needs, discover opportunities to reuse supplies, and manage their requests throughout the exchange process.

### 4.2 AI Level Up Conversational Request Assistant

The AI level-up extends request creation through a conversational chat bar. Rather than requiring students to know exactly how to describe an item or immediately complete every form field, the assistant helps turn an informal explanation into a useful search or request. The standard form remains available, allowing students to choose whichever approach suits them.

For example, a student could enter **“I need a book for English class.”** This statement communicates a general need but does not identify the correct book. The assistant would ask focused follow-up questions, such as the course code, book title, or required edition. If the student has a spending limit, it can also ask for their maximum budget. These questions help gather the information needed to distinguish a suitable item from something that only appears similar.

Once enough information is available, the assistant checks active listings for relevant matches. Unlike rigid keyword matching, this process considers the meaning of the description alongside the student’s stated requirements. A student might describe an item differently from the seller, so matching should account for related wording while still respecting details such as model, edition, and budget. Potential matches must be presented clearly so the student can review whether they meet their needs.

If a suitable listing exists, the assistant directs the student to it. This can reduce repeated searching and help students discover available items before publishing a request. However, a suggested match does not reserve the item, contact the seller, or commit the student to a purchase. The student remains responsible for reviewing the listing and deciding whether to proceed.

If no suitable listing is found, the assistant prepares a request draft using the information collected during the conversation. The student can review and edit the title, description, course code, budget, and needed-by date before posting. The draft follows the same validation rules as a manually created request, and the assistant must not invent missing details. It should also flag similar active requests already posted by that student to help prevent duplicates.

The intended benefit is less effort moving between searching and requesting. Students explain their needs once, receive help finding existing items, and can reuse that information in a request when necessary. If the AI service is unavailable, manual searching and request creation remain accessible. Price suggestions are an optional extension and would only be considered after the core conversational workflow is stable.

# Part C Development Plan

## 1 Timeline and Key Milestones (luca)

**By November 2** — Design and interface foundation. Finalize the proposal, mockups, business rules, and shared models. Establish the Kotlin Multiplatform structure, reusable Material 3 components, navigation, and initial screens for all three pillars.

**By November 16** — Core features and backend integration. Connect authentication and persistent storage. Implement listing creation and browsing, request posting and browsing, and basic messaging. Verify that records are associated with the correct accounts.

**By November 30** — Advanced features and integration. Complete advanced listing search, the conversational request assistant, and structured chat offers. Test the flow from finding or requesting an item to messaging another student. Consider optional price suggestions only after required features are stable.

**By December 7 or 8** — Final testing and submission. Resolve defects, verify responsive layouts and input validation, complete documentation and AI-use records, and rehearse the demonstration. Submit by the applicable course deadline.

## 2 Coordination and Team Commitments (Jaden)

GitHub will hold the shared codebase. Team members will work on branches and submit pull requests rather than commit directly to main. Another member must review each pull request, required builds must pass, and merge conflicts must be resolved before merging. This workflow is intended to keep main ready to build and demonstrate.

We will collaborate on written deliverables in Google Docs and export them to Word for submission. Live editing will allow team members to review and refine the same document.

We will use Microsoft Teams to share documents and communicate with the teacher, Instagram for routine team questions, and Discord for calls when a discussion would be easier in real time.

In-person meetings during or between classes will support design decisions, problem solving, and code reviews. Suitable locations include available classrooms and the computer science lounge.

When meeting in person is impractical, we may use Discord calls and screen sharing to discuss problems or work together.

At the start or end of each application development class, we will hold a brief check-in to review progress, identify blockers, confirm responsibilities, and prepare for upcoming milestones. Team members will raise significant issues early so the plan can be adjusted.

Jaden: I commit to completing the first pillar of the browsing and listing creation features on schedule to the best of my abilities. Ensuring the browsing and listing creation is robust and functional. I agree to be as available as I can for our meetings and participate in discussions along with reviewing my team’s code and notify them if I run into any big problems.

Chris: I commit to completing the second pillar of the Chat/messaging features. I will ensure that not only will it be user friendly but be fully functional and robust to the user accounts on the platform. I will complete the feature on schedule and to the best of my abilities, participate in our group discussions, and review team member code when the implementation is underway. I will also coordinate with my team to ensure the chat feature is integrated smoothly with the other listing and request features that will be developed.

Luca: I commit to completing the third pillar of the request features on schedule and to the best of my abilities. I will ensure students can create, browse, search, and manage their requests, and develop the AI chat bar to help them find existing listings or prepare request drafts. I will participate in meetings and discussions, review my teammates’ code, and communicate any major issues early. I will also coordinate with my team to ensure requests integrate smoothly with the listing and messaging features.

# Part D Risk Analysis (luca)

## Risk Register

Likelihood and consequence are rated from 1 to 3. Each risk score is calculated as likelihood multiplied by consequence, giving a range of 1 to 9.

## Listing Feature Risks

|**Risk Description**|**Risk Effect**|**Chance  <br>1 to 3**|**Impact  <br>1 to 3**|**Score  <br>1 to 9**|**Mitigation Strategy**|**Owner**|
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
|1. Asynchronous Image Loading Latency/Failure in Kamel<br><br>Remote image fetching over Ktor via Kamel (asyncPainterResource) fails or experiences high network latency when loading feed card thumbnails.|Listing feed rendering stutters or displays blank/broken image containers, degrading overall marketplace user experience.|2|2|4|Implement explicit disk/memory caching, display default local vector placeholder assets on error/loading states, and enforce strict network timeout limits.|Jaden Mayoff|
|2. KMP Compose Desktop UI Layout Scaling Inconsistencies<br><br>Adaptive layouts using BoxWithConstraints scale improperly across non-standard desktop window sizes compared to mobile displays.|Card elements overflow, text clips, or Material 3 NavigationRail / AlertDialog views misalign on larger Desktop JVM window layouts.|2|2|4|Define strict breakpoint thresholds (< 600dp mobile vs ≥ 600dp desktop), set explicit max-width and aspect-ratio constraints on cards, and test Desktop JVM builds regularly.|Jaden Mayoff|
|3. AI Search Query Parsing False Positives<br><br>The multi-parameter search parser misinterprets complex natural language queries (e.g., mistaking "Calculus 2 book" for a max budget of $2 CAD).|The feed returns irrelevant listing results or displays incorrect "Smart Search" banner tags, confusing the user.|2|1|2|Implement fallback standard keyword matching when parameter confidence is low, and render interactive filter chips so students can manually clear misparsed parameters.|Jaden Mayoff|

## Request Feature Risks

|**Risk Description**|**Risk Effect**|**Chance  <br>1 to 3**|**Impact  <br>1 to 3**|**Score  <br>1 to 9**|**Mitigation Strategy**|**Owner**|
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
|AI request assistant generates inaccurate drafts|Misinterpreted information could produce an incorrect item title, course code, or budget.|2|2|4|Ask clarifying questions, validate required fields, and require student review before posting.|Luca Maiolo|
|Low participation in the requests feed|Requests may receive few responses, reducing usefulness and discouraging students from returning.|2|2|4|Make requests accessible from Home, provide search and course filters, and promote the feature to JAC students.|Luca Maiolo|
|Unauthorized changes to requests|Incorrect permission checks could allow students to edit, delete, or close another student’s request.|2|3|6|Enforce backend ownership checks for every modification and test access using different student accounts.|Luca Maiolo|

## Messaging Feature Risks

|**Risk Description**|**Risk Effect**|**Chance  <br>1 to 3**|**Impact  <br>1 to 3**|**Score  <br>1 to 9**|**Mitigation Strategy**|**Owner**|
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
|Purchase terms are misunderstood|Unclear prices or meetup details may lead to disagreements.|2|2|4|Encourage structured Buy Requests that display the price, campus location, and agreement status. Confirm meeting times in chat.|Christopher Cardoza|
|Unauthorized access to conversations|A permission error could expose private messages to students outside the conversation.|1|3|3|Enforce backend authorization for every conversation and message. Test access with a third account.|Christopher Cardoza|
